A.explanation: The curves do not overlap, so they are not in phase. One wave reaches zero and its peak about $1\text{ s}$ before the other.

B.explanation: The $1\text{ s}$ time lag is one-eighth of the $8\text{ s}$ period, giving $(1/8) \times 360^{\circ} = 45^{\circ}$ phase difference.

C.explanation: A $90^{\circ}$ shift would need a $2\text{ s}$ lag for an $8\text{ s}$ period, but the observed lag between matching zero crossings is only $1\text{ s}$.

D.explanation: The waves are not in antiphase. A $180^{\circ}$ shift would make one positive when the other is negative with a $4\text{ s}$ lag.

Connect time lag $\Delta t$ to phase difference with $\text{phase difference} = (\Delta t / T) \times 360^{\circ}$ and compare $\Delta t$ with $T$.
walkthrough: Identify matching points on the two $s$ against $t$ curves. The larger-amplitude wave falls through $s=0$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$, while the smaller-amplitude wave falls through $s=0$ at $t = 4\text{ s}$.

Find the period $T$. The larger-amplitude wave has a peak near $t = 1\text{ s}$ and the next peak near $t = 9\text{ s}$, so $T = 9 - 1 = 8\text{ s}$. The other wave repeats over the same $8\text{ s}$.
Calculate the time lag $\Delta t$ between the waves as $\Delta t = 4 - 3 = 1\text{ s}$.
Use the phase rule that one full period is $360^{\circ}$: $\text{phase difference} = (\Delta t / T) \times 360^{\circ}$.
Substitute $\Delta t = 1\text{ s}$ and $T = 8\text{ s}$: $\text{phase difference} = (1/8) \times 360^{\circ} = 45^{\circ}$. This is option B.
